5.1 · The command deck

Three reins. One run.

Everyone knows Ctrl+C. Almost nobody knows /steer — guidance injected into a live run without breaking it. That's the difference between stopping the horse and turning it.

▎ think of it like

Reins, not a handbrake.

A galloping horse doesn't need to stop for you to change direction. You pull a rein and it turns mid-stride.

/steer
mid-run · no interruption

Injects your guidance after the next tool call. The run keeps moving; the course changes.

Use when: it's going, but drifting.
/q
queued · lands at turn end

Your message waits politely until the current turn finishes, then goes in as the next input.

Use when: it can wait a minute.
Ctrl+C
hard interrupt · now

Stops everything immediately. The blunt instrument — and usually the wrong one.

Use when: it's about to do damage.
CommandWhat it doesThe moment
/undo [N]Retract the last N turns, prefilled to retrywrong turn taken
/rollbackRestore an auto-snapshot from before a risky editit broke something
/compressSqueeze the session, optionally focused on a topiclong thread, low budget
/handoffMove a live session to another platform mid-flightleaving the desk
/moanewAsk a whole model ensemble, reasoning streamed livethe hard question
/learnnewPoint at docs or a convo → it authors a reusable skillteach it once
/journeynewPlayable timeline of its memories and skillsthe closing shot
/blueprintnewForm-based scheduled tasks — no cron syntaxautomation, gently
100K+ ★
GitHub stars in roughly three months — and Nous in funding talks at a $1.5B valuation. The commands above are why.TechCrunch · Jul 13 2026
So what →

Retire Ctrl+C as your default. Next time a run drifts, correct it with /steer — the run never breaks, and you stop paying for restarts.

5.2 · Goals that verify

It proves it's done.

Completion contracts — the agent runs your checks before it's allowed to declare victory. No more “done!” that isn't.

▎ think of it like

A building inspector.

The builder doesn't decide the house is finished. The inspector walks it, runs the checks, and signs — or doesn't.

✅
verify

How it proves it

The check the judge must see pass — tests green, files moved, page live. If you can't write the check, tighten the goal.

🚫
constraints

What it must not do

The explicit don'ts — don't touch prod, don't install packages, don't email anyone. Spoken, not assumed.

📦
boundaries

Where it may act

The blast radius — this folder, this repo, this account. Everything outside is out of bounds by contract.

a real completion contract/goal
/goal Sort every file in my Downloads into subfolders by type.
  verify: subfolders exist; no loose files left in Downloads root
  constraints: move only — never delete, never rename contents
  boundaries: ~/Downloads only
The judge in the loop

A judge rules done or continue.

After every turn, a judge model reads the contract and rules: keep going, or done. Default budget is 20 turns, then it auto-pauses. /goal status to check in, /subgoal to tighten the criteria mid-loop without restarting.

The pro move: point the judge at a cheap model. The worker thinks expensive; the referee costs pennies.

/goal status · pause · resume/subgoal20-turn budget
⏱️
Goals are not set-and-forget

A documented community run went four hours because the goal ignored its constraints and hit bot-protection walls. The fix is in the pattern: a verify clause the judge can actually check, plus a periodic /goal status. Autonomy with a leash.

So what →

Never write a bare goal again. Every /goal gets a verify clause — if you can't write the check, the agent can't pass it, and that's your signal to tighten the ask.

5.3 · Overnight self-improvement

It gets better while you sleep.

The Curator — a built-in seven-day cycle that grades, merges and prunes the agent's own skills. Zero tokens, fully deterministic.

▎ think of it like

A gardener on the night shift.

Healthy branches get tied up. Similar ones get grafted together. Dead wood gets cut. Every night, quietly.

📊Gradeevery skill scored on real usage over the week
→
🧬Consolidateoverlapping skills merged into one stronger one
→
✂️Prunedead weight cut — deterministic, zero tokens
terminal · watch it work~/.hermes
# where the cycle stands right now
$ hermes curator status

# the receipts — every grade, merge and prune
$ ls ~/.hermes/logs/curator/

# feed it: cron a weekly research run, then
$ /learn the approach we just used into a skill
🌙
Name the floors correctly

The Curator is the Hermes primitive — it ships with every install. Dream — the overnight engine you'll meet in the OS chapter — is my layer built on top of it: Curator + cron + a morning brief. Two floors, one building. Debug the primitive; enjoy the layer.

So what →

Run hermes curator status tonight so you know your baseline. Then cron one weekly job: research a topic, /learn the approach into a skill — and let the Curator keep the collection sharp.

5.4 · Proactive by default

It speaks first.

Proactivity isn't a magic toggle. It's three wires: a home channel, a schedule, and goals. Connect them and the agent starts the conversation.

▎ think of it like

A butler who knocks.

You don't summon him every time. He arrives at eight with the tray, because that's the standing arrangement.

🏠
wire 1 · the address

/sethome

The #1 beginner unlock. Without a home channel, every proactive message and cron result silently goes nowhere.

$ /sethome # in your main chat
📋
wire 2 · the schedule

/blueprint

Scheduled tasks as a form, not cron syntax. Morning brief, weekly digest, nightly check — filled in, not memorized.

💡
wire 3 · the initiative

/suggestions

The killer moment: it proposes its own automations from what it's seen you do — you just accept or dismiss.

The flagship: the intelligence brief

A morning brief that improves itself.

Email + calendar connected (read and draft — never send), one blueprint, and every morning it tells you what's landed, what's on, and what to focus on.

The twist that makes it compound: once a week it interviews you about the brief — and rewrites its own prompt based on your answers.

read + draft onlyweekly self-reviewsaved my bacon
the brief prompt · paste once
Every morning: check my email and calendar.
Tell me what came in, what's on today, and
what to focus on.

Once a week: interview me on how good the
brief was and how it could be better — then
improve the next one based on my answers.
🔍
Honesty beat: there is no “proactive mode” switch

A configurable check-in mode is still an open feature request, not a shipped toggle. Today, proactivity = cron + home channel + goals. That's not a limitation — it's the recipe.

So what →

/sethome tonight, then paste the brief prompt above. Give email read and draft only — the agent that can't send can't embarrass you.

5.5 · Subagents & the board

One brain. A team of hands.

Quick parallel jobs go to delegate_task. Real orchestration — named workers, gated hand-offs, work that survives a crash — lives on the Kanban board.

▎ think of it like

A dispatch office.

Jobs go up on the board. Couriers take them in parallel. The last card waits, by rule, until both deliveries land.

Kanban boardasync · named · survives crashes
  • Named worker profiles take cards in parallel, dispatcher runs the flow
  • Cards gate on parents — synthesize waits until both researches land
  • Survives restarts, fully auditable, live board at 127.0.0.1:9119
  • Human-in-the-loop: a worker blocks a card, you comment, it resumes
delegate_tasksync · anonymous · fire-and-return
  • Spawns background subagents, results consolidated back to the parent
  • The child knows nothing except the goal and context you pass — isolation by design
  • Concurrency of 3 — quick fan-outs, not long campaigns
  • Watch live cost, tokens and kill-switches per subagent on /agents
🔬
card 1 + 2
Fan out

research-NA and research-EU run in parallel, one named worker each.

⛩️
card 3
The gate

synthesize is blocked on both parents — by rule, not by hope.

✍️
auto
Promote

Both land → the writer card promotes itself and runs.

🌙
tomorrow
Remember

The nightly ops card reads yesterday's metadata — the team that remembers.

So what →

Run one fan-out this week: two research workers, one gated synthesize card — and keep the board open at 127.0.0.1:9119. Watching it dispatch is the moment orchestration clicks.

5.6 · The speed drops

Quietly, it got fast.

Two upgrades you barely notice and never stop benefiting from: tool calls in parallel, and web research that stopped dawdling.

▎ think of it like

Four lanes, no queue.

It used to call Gmail, then calendar, then search — single file. Now they all run at once.

🐌
Beforeone call at a time
  • Tools called one after another
  • Web research: scrape the page, pay a second model to summarize it
  • ~3 minutes per research question
⚡
Nowparallel + direct
  • Email, calendar, weather, search — one simultaneous beat
  • Web search reads direct: ~60× faster, ~49× cheaper
  • ~15 seconds for the same answer
The speed dividenddrag it · your day, before vs after
6
16 min
waiting time returned per day
101 hrs
per year — at ~49× lower search cost
Basis: ~3 min old flow vs ~15 s new flow per research task — Hermes' published 60×/49× figures.
🔥
Stack Firecrawl on top

Point research through Firecrawl and pages arrive as clean text — no ads, no HTML noise, ~93% of tokens saved on a scrape. It even extracts a site's brand identity: logo, colors, fonts. That's how one vague prompt turns into an on-brand deliverable.

So what →

First, update: just tell Hermes “update to the latest version” — it updates itself. Then give it one four-things-at-once request and watch the lanes fill.

5.7 · Two tools, one stack

It wraps Claude Code.

Not a rivalry — a hierarchy. Hermes is the always-on operator; Claude Code is the master craftsman it hires for the deep work.

▎ think of it like

The operator and the contractor.

The operator runs your world all day. When a job needs a specialist, it hires one — and keeps the receipts.

Hermespersistent runtime · the operator
  • Always-on server runtime — lives across sessions, speaks every channel
  • /steer injects mid-run without breaking it — a genuinely novel primitive
  • Kanban + cron are first-class — orchestration is built in, not bolted on
  • Spawns Claude Code as a subagent and folds the results into its memory
Claude Codein-repo session · the craftsman
  • Deepest coding craft — the specialist you want inside a repo
  • Steering = Esc and re-prompt — the run breaks, then restarts
  • Scheduling and orchestration need external wrapping
  • CLAUDE.md is user-maintained — you curate what it knows

The lovely footnote: both tools independently converged on lifecycle hooks invisible to the model. When two teams land on the same architecture, that's the architecture.

So what →

Stop choosing. Hermes delegates the code to Claude Code and keeps the memory — the operator remembers what the contractor built, forever.

5.8 · The traps

Nine ways beginners stall.

Every one of these is a real support message. Pin the list — it's the difference between “Hermes is broken” and “oh, that's me.”

No home channel
the classic

Cron fires, proactive messages send — into the void. /sethome first, always.

Aux model unset
silent degrade

Vision, compression and the /goal judge quietly limp until the auxiliary model is configured.

Memory ≠ skills
wrong drawer

Memory = facts. Skills = procedures. And edits apply next session — the snapshot is frozen by design.

Fire-and-forget goals
budget burn

A judge false-negative can eat the 20-turn budget. Check /goal status; tighten with /subgoal.

Ollama's 4,096 default
local trap

The default context silently cripples agent loops. Set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH before blaming the model.

GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS
never

That flag hands your agent — and its keys — to anyone who finds the bot. Allowlists, always.

Chat surfaces burn 2–3×
cost drift

Telegram and friends cost 2–3× the tokens of the CLI. Do heavy work at the terminal.

/model mid-session
cache nuke

Switching models mid-run invalidates the prompt cache — the next turn costs full price.

The giant backpack
docs' own words

Don't pile every workflow into the default profile. One reliable workflow at a time.

So what →

Screenshot this grid. Nine out of ten “it's not working” messages in the community are one of these nine — and every fix is under a minute.

You have the levers.
